newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Americans, Italians airlifted from anarchic Albania.
newsitem.headline: Americans, Italians airlifted from anarchic Albania.

text.p: Military helicopters mounted a dramatic airlift of hundreds of Americans and Europeans from the anarchy of Albania on Friday as small arms fire crackled through the streets of Tirana.
European envoy Franz Vranitzky began talks with Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino aboard the Italian frigate Aliseo in the Adriatic and rebel leaders were due to join later.

Vranitzky, who represents the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, and Fino were flown to the warship by helicopter. Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Yannos Kranidiotis also plans to join the talks.
Vranitzky said he would urge the European Union and OSCE member states to give serious thought to a request from Tirana to send in military support to Albania.
Speaking to Reuters by telephone from the Aliseo, he said he believed order could only be restored in Albania with outside help.

Officials at a military hospital in the Albanian capital said a total of three people, including a four-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, were killed and 72 injured by stray bullets overnight. Local media said more than 100 people had died since the unrest erupted earlier this month.
As looting persisted in Tirana on Friday, with supermarkets and building sites the latest targets, the government appealed to policemen and soldiers to report for duty.
In further evidence of growing lawlessness, one man carrying a rifle was gunned down in a Tirana street by four men who drove by in a van, witnesses said.

Giant twin-rotored Chinook military helicopters airlifted about 100 Italians from Tirana's football stadium soon after dawn on Friday, completing an Italian evacuation of about 1,000 of its nationals.

American Sea Knight and Sea Stallion helicopters flew from U.S. Navy amphibious ships in the Adriatic to rescue up to 2,200 Americans from the embassy housing complex in Tirana, while Cobra escort helicopters circled overhead.
U.S. marines were securing the operation on the ground, a spokesman said.

"We have so far evacuated more than 200 people during the day and another 51 last night. The operation is going very smoothly. The aim is to get out of Albania as quickly as possible," said U.S. Army Major Dave Daigle, a spokesman at the European Command headquarters in Stuttgart.
As the Americans flew out, U.S. ambassador Marisa Lino appeared on Albanian television to assure Albanians that the United States was not abandoning them.
"The United States of America is not leaving Albania," she said. "I and some of my team will remain."
France sent four helicopters to increasingly-chaotic Albania on Friday to evacuate French nationals and those of several other countries from the port of Durres.
Britain said it had evacuated 131 people from Albania on Friday morning and they were on their way to the Italian Adriatic Sea port of Brindisi in an Italian naval ship.
The Greek frigate "Kavaloudis" evacuated 49 people -- 44 Greeks and five Belgians -- from the Albanian port of Durres, west of Tirana, on Friday, defence ministry officials said.

At least 14 Albanian navy craft, most of them small patrol boats built nearly 50 years ago by the Chinese, limped into southern Italian ports under Italian navy escort after crossing the southern Adriatic with deserting servicemen and civilians.
Former Albanian Defence Minister Safet Zhulali and his family arrived in Italy on a merchant ship on Friday with about 70 other people fleeing the chaos in their homeland.
Zhulali was replaced as minister by Socialist Shaqir Vukaj in a newly formed coalition government this week. Two of President Sali Berisha's children fled to Ialy on Thursday.
The European Union said it was working closely with the OSCE and NATO on a coordinated urgent response to the deepening crisis in Albania.
Tanks were absent from the streets of the Albanian capital on Friday morning. They had been sent out late on Thursday to help stem the virtual anarchy gripping Albania.
Albania's chaotic revolt, which began in the south where people lost their savings in collapsed pyramid investment schemes, has spread to the north of the country since mid-week.

Albania's government called for foreign military intervention to halt the disorder, but German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the crisis was essentially an internal matter and it was not clear what foreign troops would do there.
